reading.rtitle: Small Talk on the Ward -- A Guide for International Graduates
paras: WHY IT MATTERS. In American hospitals, small talk is not wasted time. Two minutes about the weather or the weekend before a case discussion tell your colleagues that you are easy to work with. Many international graduates are excellent clinicians but come across as cold, simply because they go straight to the point. A short question like It's been a busy morning, hasn't it? is enough to break the ice.

SOFTENING. American colleagues rarely give orders, even when they are in charge. Instead of Give me the chart, they say Could you grab the chart for me? or Would you mind sending me the note? Speakers of other languages often sound blunt in English without meaning it. A question tag can soften a request too: You couldn't check room four for me, could you?

READING THE CUES. Americans often say what they mean indirectly. Let's touch base later usually means that the conversation is over for now. A heads-up is a polite warning: Just a heads-up, the family in room six is upset. When somebody says No worries, the problem is really closed. And when a colleague says We should hang out sometime, it is friendly, but it is not always an invitation with a date.

WHAT TO AVOID. Some topics are awkward at work: salary, religion, politics and weight. A safer list is plans, food, sports and travel. If a silence feels awkward, ask a question about the other person. Most Americans are happy to chat about themselves, and they will remember you as the resident who asked.
reading.source: Teaching guide written for this lesson about American workplace communication. The habits and the vocabulary are the target; it is not the guide of any real hospital.

listenings.text: Every July I watch the new international residents, and the ones who struggle are rarely the ones with weak medicine. They are the ones who go straight to the point. In this hospital, a case discussion starts with thirty seconds of small talk. Long night, wasn't it? You're on call again on Friday, aren't you? Nobody expects a real answer. It is a way of saying: I see you, and we are on the same team. The second thing is requests. If you say give me the labs, people hear an order, even if you mean it politely. Say could you send me the labs, or you couldn't send me the labs, could you? It sounds small, but the nurses will remember. And the third thing: listen for the cues. When I say let's touch base tomorrow, I am closing the conversation. When I give you a heads-up, I am telling you something important without making it dramatic. Learn those three things, and your English will sound a lot more American than your accent ever will.

In my first month I had a reputation, and I did not know it. A nurse told me later that people thought I was rude. I was surprised, because I was trying hard to be efficient. I said things like: bring me the chart, call the family, the patient in bed two needs a dressing. In my language that is normal between colleagues. Here it sounded blunt. The nurse who told me was kind about it. She gave me a heads-up over coffee, and she said: you're a good doctor, you know that, don't you? But you need to soften it a little. So I started adding could you and would you mind. I started asking the nurses about their weekends. It felt awkward for about two weeks. Then it was just how I talked. Last month a new resident asked me how I had become so popular with the nursing staff. I told him: small talk, and the word please.

extra_audio.text: Hi, I'm Diego, one of the new residents. It's been a long morning, hasn't it? I'm going to grab a coffee before clinic. Just a heads-up, the printer on the third floor isn't working. We should hang out after work one day this week. Let's touch base after the afternoon session, shall we?
